Both hold because the refusal of a repair lives at the one place that can know a repair would be needed before any Log sees the store. Rejected: opening a read-only log at its pinned head and reporting the repair as pending (a Log mode, and a served state the store has not reconciled); a read-only mode on Log or Anchor; making read-only opening a LeafStore trait method, which would add a criterion to BACKENDS.md; and a per-leaf hash record so a refusal could name the changed leaf.
consequences: StoreError gains ReadOnly and RepairPending; no existing variant changes.
The LeafStore trait and BACKENDS.md are unchanged, so a second backend owes no read-only open.
A changed leaf is refused as PinMismatch from Log::open, naming no leaf index; FileLeafStore::leaf serves unchecked bytes and a leaf is proven whole only through Log::open.
Readers that must not write (Anchor::open_read_only, the lys log commands) are moved onto open_read_only by a further unit; until then they still repair on a read path.
LYSLOGSTORE-002 is cut back to the witness, and its line that Log and Anchor gain no read-only mode stands.

decisions.title: The given statement is a lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 bytes of lys.given's data, its hash kept in the render manifest, written only when render-launch is given a key
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the given-statement card, with the lead's answers of 28 September on where the hash is recorded, the refusal message and the certificate check; the canonical form and the statement's keeping chosen by HOME-022's author and proposed with that brief
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.5 asks that what an agent was given be a signed statement checked with lys verify --attestation. The lys.given entry records the hashes of the documents a session was given and no hash of itself, lys-core's attestation signs SHA-256 of a payload, and a signed form is frozen from its first signature, so the bytes signed have to be named so a stranger can rebuild them with standard tooling, and the hash has to sit in a record a stranger reading the session can find.
decisions.decision: The given statement is lys-core's existing lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) bytes of the lys.given entry's data. The SHA-256 of those bytes, the given hash, is recorded in every render's manifest block as given_sha256 and printed in the render-launch report; the template_render event keeps the shape ADR-012 decided and names the manifest by hash. The statement is written only when render-launch is given a key: kept as a block named by a lys.given_statement entry hung under the lys.given entry, and as given-statement.cose and given-data.json under --out for lys verify. Rejected: serialising the record in struct field order, which a stranger cannot rebuild without the Rust type; signing the 64-hex hash string, whose attested hash would be SHA-256 of the hex and not the given hash; adding the given hash to the template_render event's detail, which changes the shape ADR-012 decided; recording it only in the report, where a stranger reading the session cannot find it; keeping the COSE bytes inline as hex in the entry rather than as a block; and adding the file's path to lys verify's one failure message, which would change the published lys for every user.
consequences: docs/design/home/RECORD.md states the staged import's rule beside the per-append durability order, which is unchanged for every other append.

Only an import into a session it creates is staged; import_claude_code given a session that is already open keeps append_entry's per-entry syncs, since a rename cannot publish a session that already exists.
Reconcile is not extended and no session file is trimmed, rewritten or truncated; recovering a session whose last line a crash tore is its own decision.
A staging file does not end in `.jsonl`, so Home::session_ids never lists it as a session.
The block store's two syncs per new block are unchanged and are not part of the import's bounded count; they are counted beside it.
The RFC 8785 form of lys.given's data is a wire contract from the first signature; changing it means a new statement type alongside, never a mutation.
Every render manifest carries given_sha256, keyed or not; the template_render event and the lys.given entry are unchanged.
A render with no key writes the lys.given entry as HOME-003 records it and no statement, and says unsigned.

The statement signs what a session was given, not which session: equal lys.given data gives equal payloads, and the tie to a session is the lys.given_statement entry's unsigned place under its lys.given entry.

The statement is checked with the unchanged lys verify; which key signed is checked by comparing its signer public key with an expected key until row 6.1 supplies a certificate over the home's key for lys verify --cert.
The start statement and the role-move statement are later statements over the START launch record and the ROLES version record, written when those records land.

decisions.title: A Claude Code import builds its session under a staging name and publishes it once
decisions.decided_by: The home line's lead, answering the survey of the repeated-work card; recorded with HOME-020
decisions.context: Every imported entry went through Session::append_entry, which syncs the line, syncs the index row and writes the head through a temporary file, a rename and a directory sync: about five syncs per record, though the import sets the head once at its end. Appending in place with no sync until the end cannot be repaired by the existing reconcile: a crash can leave a torn or zero-filled last line that Index::scan refuses as Malformed, so the session will not open, a head still at the header, and a re-import refused as Exists; and the original bytes are never rewritten (P1), so a torn tail cannot be trimmed.
decisions.decision: The import command builds its new session under the staging name `<id>.jsonl.importing` beside `sessions/<id>.jsonl`, holding `<id>.lock` throughout: the header and every entry line are written to the staging file with no sync, and the index rows and the head are kept in memory. It then publishes once, in this order: one sync of the staging file; the index written whole to `<id>.index.jsonl` through a temporary file, synced and renamed; the head written once to `<id>.head` through a temporary file, synced and renamed; one sync of the sessions directory; the staging file renamed to `<id>.jsonl`; one more sync of the sessions directory. A crash before the rename leaves no session under the final name, so a re-import is not refused as Exists; the next import of that id and the next open of that session file, each holding the lock, remove the staging file and, when `<id>.jsonl` is absent, the `<id>.index.jsonl` and `<id>.head` a part-way publish left. Rejected: appending in place and leaving a session that refuses by name after a crash; extending reconcile to trim an unsynced tail.
consequences: The LeafStore trait gains no method, and BACKENDS.md and the second backend's adoption criteria do not change.
Log, Log::open, its one-leaf repair, StoreError::PinMismatch and the anchor do not change; a writable open repairs an interrupted append as before.
A handle from open_read_only never writes: tests hold every file under the store, dot-prefixed names included, to the same bytes before and after each refusal.
RepairPending is decided without reading a leaf, and a test proves it with a counter on the read path of leaf files.
ADR-101's rejection of a read-only open of a refused log stands: open_read_only refuses a store past its pin instead of serving it.
docs/design/home/RECORD.md states the staged import's rule beside the per-append durability order, which is unchanged for every other append.

Only an import into a session it creates is staged; import_claude_code given a session that is already open keeps append_entry's per-entry syncs, since a rename cannot publish a session that already exists.
Reconcile is not extended and no session file is trimmed, rewritten or truncated; recovering a session whose last line a crash tore is its own decision.
A staging file does not end in `.jsonl`, so Home::session_ids never lists it as a session.
The block store's two syncs per new block are unchanged and are not part of the import's bounded count; they are counted beside it.

decisions.title: The server judges a grant's standing and effective end over its chain; the screens render them and walk nothing
decisions.decided_by: The lead for the identity line, in answer to the grant-rows conformance survey; recorded with DIRECTORY-035
decisions.context: The identity screens decided whether a grant stands by walking its chain in the browser (model.ts standing(), with its own clock), while the service decides the same question when a grant is exercised. Rejected: keeping the client chain walk beside the server's judgement, and a screen-side derivation of the effective end.
consequences: Any screen that shows whether a grant stands reads GrantView.standing and nothing else; a client standing derivation is a review finding.

decisions.title: The given statement is a lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 bytes of lys.given's data, its hash kept in the render manifest, written only when render-launch is given a key
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the given-statement card, with the lead's answers of 28 September on where the hash is recorded, the refusal message and the certificate check; the canonical form and the statement's keeping chosen by HOME-022's author and proposed with that brief
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.5 asks that what an agent was given be a signed statement checked with lys verify --attestation. The lys.given entry records the hashes of the documents a session was given and no hash of itself, lys-core's attestation signs SHA-256 of a payload, and a signed form is frozen from its first signature, so the bytes signed have to be named so a stranger can rebuild them with standard tooling, and the hash has to sit in a record a stranger reading the session can find.
decisions.decision: The given statement is lys-core's existing lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) bytes of the lys.given entry's data. The SHA-256 of those bytes, the given hash, is recorded in every render's manifest block as given_sha256 and printed in the render-launch report; the template_render event keeps the shape ADR-012 decided and names the manifest by hash. The statement is written only when render-launch is given a key: kept as a block named by a lys.given_statement entry hung under the lys.given entry, and as given-statement.cose and given-data.json under --out for lys verify. Rejected: serialising the record in struct field order, which a stranger cannot rebuild without the Rust type; signing the 64-hex hash string, whose attested hash would be SHA-256 of the hex and not the given hash; adding the given hash to the template_render event's detail, which changes the shape ADR-012 decided; recording it only in the report, where a stranger reading the session cannot find it; keeping the COSE bytes inline as hex in the entry rather than as a block; and adding the file's path to lys verify's one failure message, which would change the published lys for every user.
consequences: The RFC 8785 form of lys.given's data is a wire contract from the first signature; changing it means a new statement type alongside, never a mutation.
Every render manifest carries given_sha256, keyed or not; the template_render event and the lys.given entry are unchanged.
A render with no key writes the lys.given entry as HOME-003 records it and no statement, and says unsigned.

The statement signs what a session was given, not which session: equal lys.given data gives equal payloads, and the tie to a session is the lys.given_statement entry's unsigned place under its lys.given entry.

The statement is checked with the unchanged lys verify; which key signed is checked by comparing its signer public key with an expected key until row 6.1 supplies a certificate over the home's key for lys verify --cert.

decisions.title: lys enforces its code rules with ast-grep, recognising test code by structure the file carries
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in the rulings to the ast-grep card's runs 04213a71, 0d44242f and 6747ce61; recorded with LYSCORE-003
decisions.context: The lys gate had no ast-grep leg, so its rules against unwrap, expect and panic outside tests, against lint bypasses, against dropped Results and against logic in mod.rs held only where clippy overlapped them. Cambium's rule set carries no unwrap rule and forbids every #[allow], while lys CLAUDE.md sanctioned a per-module #![allow] opt-out for tests. An unwrap rule has to tell test code from library code, and 224 calls at 4dd1c33 sat in fixture.rs files and in helper fns of *_tests.rs files, none of which carried an in-file test marker.
decisions.decision: Carry Cambium's mod-rs-declarations-only, no-let-underscore-on-results and no-lint-bypass-attributes, and add lys's own no-unwrap-expect-panic-outside-tests. That rule treats as test code a file whose first item is #![cfg(test)], a #[cfg(test)] mod body, a #[test] fn body, and a path under tests/. Every *_tests.rs file, both fixture.rs files, every integration test root and both tests/harness/mod.rs files gain #![cfg(test)] as their first line. The per-module #![allow] opt-outs are replaced by clippy.toml's allow-unwrap-in-tests, allow-expect-in-tests and allow-panic-in-tests. Every existing hit is fixed at its cause in the same card, so the leg is green when it lands. The leg `ast-grep scan --config sgconfig.yml` runs in docs/design/project.json, .land/gates.sh and CI. Rejected: an exemption list of file names; rewriting the calls in test files; narrowing no-lint-bypass-attributes to spare the test opt-outs; carrying only the rules that were clean at the time.
consequences: A new sibling *_tests.rs, fixture file or integration test root begins with #![cfg(test)], or the unwrap rule reports its helper calls and clippy refuses them.
No #[allow] remains in the tree; an #[allow] outside tests is fixed at its cause, and one that cannot be is brought to the lead as a question with its line.
CLAUDE.md and Cargo.toml name clippy.toml in place of the per-module #![allow].
Every carried rule is at severity error, and the leg fails the gate on any hit.
The leg needs a gate venue that declares tool:ast-grep.

decisions.title: A rule that cannot fire on the lys tree is not carried

decisions.title: The 500-line limit on code files is a gate leg, not a sentence in CLAUDE.md
decisions.decided_by: Tom's word in the terminal on 28 September 2026; recorded by Waffles with LYSGATE-002
decisions.context: CLAUDE.md's coding standards say no file holds over 500 lines of code, excluding tests, comments and whitespace. No gate leg measures it: not project.json, not a cluster gate, not .land/gates.sh, not CI. On main 6194599 the largest code files are 498 lines, so the rule holds today by care alone, and a build could land a 700-line file through every gate.
decisions.decision: A gate leg, `sh scripts/file-length.sh`, runs the checker's own tests and then measures every tracked Rust and TypeScript source file, and fails naming each file whose code lines exceed 500. It is declared in project.json, in every cluster design.json gate, in .land/gates.sh, in CLAUDE.md's 'Gates before any commit' block and in CI. Rejected: an ast-grep rule, which matches syntax and cannot count lines; a clippy lint, since too_many_lines counts one function, not a file, and says nothing of TypeScript; counting raw lines, which would punish documentation.
decisions.quote: Make sure everything follows the ast-grep scan rules. Make sure that no files are over 500 lines of code. Make sure it is all fully finished and make sure it actually works and meets the point of doing it. No lazy code, nothing replaying, nothing taking extra time, no unnecessary clones. It all has to work as efficiently as possible because this is going to be running in the background of absolutely everything.
consequences: A file over the limit is refused in the build's own round, not found later at landing or by a reader.
The count is defined once, in the checker, with its tests beside it; CLAUDE.md's sentence points at the leg.
Splitting a file that grows past 500 lines is the build's work in the round it grows, never a follow-up card.

decisions.title: Lys hot paths do each piece of work once: no replay, no whole-state read for a sliver, no clone to read, no blocking on an async worker
decisions.decided_by: Tom's word in the terminal on 28 September 2026; recorded by Waffles with HOME-035, DIRECTORY-042, DIRECTORY-043, SECRETS-005 and LYSLOGSTORE-005
decisions.context: Read-only efficiency audit of main 9712505 on 28 September 2026, each finding confirmed by an independent reviewer that tried to refute it; findings kept in the brief's requirements with their file and line. 26 findings were confirmed across lys-home, lys-identity, lys-identity-server, lys-secrets and lys-log-store.
decisions.decision: Work on a request, append or open path is done once and scales with what the caller touches, not with history: lookups by index instead of scans, a checkpoint or cursor instead of a replay, a filtered read instead of the whole set, borrowed data instead of a clone made to read, one fsync per batch instead of per entry, and blocking I/O and std mutexes kept off async workers. Each fix is proved by counting the work done in a test that fails before it, never by a clock.
decisions.quote: Make sure there's no lazy code in there. Nothing replaying, nothing taking extra time, no unnecessary clones. It all has to work as efficiently as possible because this is going to be running in the background of absolutely everything.
consequences: A finding of this kind is a defect with a card, not a follow-up.
Tests that count work (reads, parses, scans, fsyncs, lock acquisitions) become the regression guard, since a clock is not allowed in a test.
The 5 second timeouts in the SpiceDB client are removed with its rewrite.

decisions.title: The identity install and its clients wait on signals, never on a clock
decisions.decided_by: Tom's standing rules (CLAUDE.md 'No time limits'; 24 September 2026, waits are on signals, never on a clock); recorded by Waffles with DIRECTORY-044
decisions.context: On main f003aff the lys identity install polls its services with thread::sleep (install/services.rs:149, :229, :315) and each loopback exchange, the Rauthy client and the health check carry fixed timeouts (loopback_http.rs, rauthy.rs:21, health.rs:23, services.rs:298). The identity shell's Explain view re-measures on a 120 ms timer. Each is a bound in seconds or a wait on a clock.
decisions.decision: A wait ends on the event it is waiting for or on the failure that makes the event impossible: a service is ready when it says so or when a single connection to it succeeds after a readiness event (its log gaining its listening line, observed through the platform's file-change notification), a stopped process is gone when the platform reports its exit (kqueue EVFILT_PROC on macOS, pidfd on Linux), a peer that refuses or closes is an error at once, and nothing carries a timeout. The screen re-measures on a ResizeObserver or animation-frame signal. Rejected: shorter sleeps, which still wait on a clock; keeping timeouts as a safety net, which the rule forbids and which hides a stuck peer's cause.
decisions.quote: No timeout, deadline, watchdog or bound in seconds anywhere: not in code, not in a test, not in a workflow step, not in a command. A slow run is a defect to find at its cause. Something stuck is found by its signal (no progress, a dead process), never by a clock.
consequences: A service that never becomes ready and never exits leaves the install waiting and saying what it waits on; its cause is found from its log, never cut off by a clock.
Interaction timings on the screen that are behaviour, not waits (how long a notice stays shown, the window for a two-key chord), are not time limits and stay.

decisions.title: An installed identity product names its build and upgrades itself in place, keeping the previous build to return to
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, under Tom's word on 28 September 2026 that it must actually work and meet the point of doing it; recorded with DIRECTORY-045
decisions.context: On 28 September 2026 at 17:1x the live install on Tom's Mac (~/Library/Application Support/lys/identity) ran a server built at 15:12. `lys-identity-server --version` answered ConfigInvalid (it read --version as a config path), so nothing on the machine could say which commit it was, and `lys identity install` run again 'changes only what is missing; nothing is rotated or restarted' (crates/lys/src/identity/install.rs:1-9), so the product has no way to take a newer build. Every landing after an install is invisible to the person using it until someone hand-replaces binaries.
decisions.decision: Every Lys binary answers --version with the commit and dirty state it was built from, stamped at build time; a build with no commit to read says so in those words, never a made-up value. `lys identity upgrade` takes a folder of newly built binaries (and optionally a screens package), checks each one's --version, stops the service and the broker by their exit events, swaps the binaries by rename keeping the previous set beside them, starts the new ones and waits for them ready; if any new binary fails to start or become ready, it puts the previous set back, starts it, and fails naming what broke. Data, credentials, configuration and the compose services are never touched by an upgrade. Rejected: making install restart what differs, which would mix a first install's promises with an upgrade's risks; asking people to copy binaries by hand.
decisions.quote: Make sure it is all fully finished and make sure it actually works and meets the point of doing it.
consequences: A landing reaches a running install by one command, and the running build can always be named.
A bad build never leaves the install down: the previous build comes back and the failure is named.

decisions.title: Lys is the only sign-in a person or a product ever sees; the issuer inside it is never shown
decisions.decided_by: Tom, 28 September 2026 about 19:10 Melbourne; recorded by Waffles with DIRECTORY-047
decisions.context: On 28 September 2026 the live install sent Tom to the issuer's own sign-in page at localhost:18080 with the issuer's branding, kept the administrator in the issuer's admin site, took the administrator's email from a flag Archie filled from the machine's git user.email (an address Tom must never see), and asked him to read a password file in Terminal. Cambium was registered as a client of the issuer, not of Lys. Tom could not sign in for an hour.
decisions.decision: Lys is the single sign-on for every product: every product is a client of Lys at Lys's own origin, and no product configuration names the issuer. A person meets only Lys screens: first-run setup, sign-in, provider setup and their own account are Lys pages, and the issuer's pages, admin site, name and password files are never part of any path a person follows. First run asks the person for the administrator's name, email and password; nothing is filled from the machine.
decisions.quote: Lys is meant to be the sign-in for everything. It's meant to be our only own single sign-on for absolutely everything. Cambium uses Lys, not Rauthy. / How is an average person supposed to do it?
consequences: The service speaks to the issuer server-side for password sign-in, provider sign-in, account changes and administration.
The issuer's admin site is not reachable from a browser on the host.
Install output and every refusal a person reads name Lys, never the issuer.
Replacing the issuer later changes no product.

decisions.title: Every app registers with Lys through one published API; Lys depends on no app
decisions.decided_by: Tom, 28 September 2026 evening; recorded by Waffles with DIRECTORY-048 and DIRECTORY-049
decisions.context: Lys holds one permission model read from a file at start (grant_model_file: relations and their actions) and accepts any resource kind a grant names, so no app can declare what its resources are, which actions they carry or how they nest, and nothing stops two apps using the same kind name. There is no registration of an app as a product: its sign-in client (DIRECTORY-047 R3) and its permissions are unrelated. There is no published description of the API, and no MCP server: the design mock-up lists 'identity (this service)' among every agent's MCP servers, and nothing serves it.
decisions.decision: An app is a record in Lys: an id, a name, its sign-in client, and a permission schema it owns (resource kinds under the app's own prefix, each kind's actions, relations carrying actions, and parent kinds whose relations flow down). An app registers and changes its schema only through the API, is approved by an administrator on a Lys screen before it has any effect, and cannot touch another app's kinds. Lys's own model is the schema of the app 'lys'. The API is described by one OpenAPI document generated from the routes and their types, never written by hand. The MCP server is a face over that same API with three tools, the caller's own identity on every call, and no credential or authority of its own. Lys depends on no app. It holds no app's name, kind, schema or code; it never calls an app, waits on one or reads one's store. Every app depends on Lys through this API alone, and Lys runs the same with no apps registered as with twenty.
decisions.quote: a quality API as well, because we're going to need a way of getting in the permission schema and everything for every one of the apps that it covers / this has to be able to handle sign in and authentication and permissions for every single one of our apps, but not depend on them / it will need to be secure and compact
consequences: Adding an app changes no Lys code and no Lys configuration file.
A schema change that would strand standing grants is refused by name, never applied with a silent revoke.
The MCP server and the HTTP API can never disagree: one route table, one set of handlers, one grant check.
No app outage, slowness or removal changes any Lys answer about another app or about Lys itself.

decisions.title: Lys runs the agents it starts: its own background terminal, or a runner another tool provides
decisions.decided_by: Tom, 28 September 2026 19:48 Melbourne, on Dot; recorded by Waffles with DIRECTORY-050
decisions.context: Lys renders an agent's start command from its kept profile and records the start (launch_api.rs, start.rs), but never runs it: the command is handed to a person or another tool. Sessions report starting, running and stopped themselves (runtime_api.rs), and an emergency stop asks each session's runtime to end it (stop_api.rs). Running, typing into and reading agent sessions is done outside Lys today by Argus through herdr and, as designed, by Manifold, neither of which Lys can rely on.
decisions.decision: Lys runs the agents it starts. A runner is the part that holds an agent's terminal: Lys ships one of its own, a background process on each machine that runs each started agent in its own pseudo-terminal, and accepts any other runner that speaks the same small, published runner protocol. Through a runner, Lys starts, types into, presses keys in, reads, waits on, resizes, compacts and stops a session, rotates it across its accounts when it reports a usage limit, and wakes it with a message, each act under the caller's grants and recorded. Lys depends on no particular runner: its own is the default, another is chosen per machine.
decisions.quote: I've decided that I want this to actually handle the launching of agents, either through a background terminal of its own or plugging into something else. I want it to be able to do all of the things that Argus can do currently through herdr, and what was supposed to be done through manifold.
consequences: An agent can be started, driven and stopped entirely from Lys's screens, API and MCP, with no other tool installed.
Argus and Manifold may become runners or clients of Lys; neither is required by it.
Every keystroke or message sent to a session is an act under a grant, with a receipt.
The earlier rule that Lys gives a start command and never runs the agent is superseded for machines with a runner; a machine with none still gets the command.

decisions.title: Lys tracks every agent session's tokens, context, time, budgets and goals; Argus's job moves into Lys, in Rust
decisions.decided_by: Tom, 28 September 2026 19:50 to 19:51 Melbourne, on Dot; recorded by Waffles with DIRECTORY-051
decisions.context: Argus, a separate service, watches agent sessions: context use and budgets, compaction requests, goal reminders and scheduled messages, reaching sessions through herdr. Tom: it keeps crashing and cannot track budgets, token usage, time and goals through Lys. Lys already keeps each session's home and transcript (lys-home) and, with DIRECTORY-050, runs the session.
decisions.decision: Lys measures each session it runs from the harness's own transcript: tokens in and out per turn, context in use against the model's window, time running, and the account each turn was paid from. A budget is set on an agent, a team or a person, for context, tokens and time, and Lys acts when one is reached: compacts at a context threshold, stops at a hard token or time cap, or tells the responsible person. Goals are records on an agent with a deadline and reminders Lys delivers into the session through its runner. Everything is under grants, on screens, in the API and in receipts; nothing depends on Argus.
decisions.quote: Argus is not going to be able to do what we need, to be able to track budgets and token usage, time, goals and everything like that through Lys. We're going to completely rewrite that, in Rust.
consequences: Argus is retired once Lys does what it does for our sessions; nothing in Lys calls it.
A budget is only called a hard cap where Lys can stop the session that breaches it.
Usage is measured from the transcript Lys keeps, never from a session's own claim.
